claim: Hyperoxia represents the single most important toxic exposure to premature neonatal lungs and is the key risk factor for chronic lung disease of prematurity or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD).
source: Hyperoxia represents the single most important toxic exposure to premature neonatal lungs and is the key risk factor for chronic lung disease of prematurity or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (Jobe and Bancalari, 2001; Peek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jobe and Bancalari, 2001 and Peek et al., 2017

claim: Almost 40% of infants born at <29 weeks of gestation (approximately 10,000 new cases in USA each year) suffer from BPD.
source: Despite remarkable improvements in the survival of premature neonates, almost 40% of infants born at <29 weeks of gestation (approximately 10,000 new cases in USA each year) suffer from BPD (Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Neonatal Research Network et al., 2010; Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Neonatal Research Network et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Neonatal Research Network et al., 2010 and 2015

claim: In surviving adults, BPD is associated with an increased risk of respiratory infections, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
source: In surviving adults, BPD is associated with an increased risk of respiratory infections, such as asthma (Gough et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Islam et al., 2015; McGrath-Morrow and Collaco, 2019; Savran and Ulrik, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on asthma and COPD associations

claim: Neonatal hyperoxia increased morbidity from influenza A virus (IAV) in a murine model in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In a murine model, neonatal hyperoxia increased morbidity from influenza A virus (IAV) (O'Reilly et al., 2008) in a dose-dependent manner (Maduekwe et al., 2015) through pathways involving both alveolar type 2 (AT2) epithelial cells and immune pathways (Buczynski et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Reilly et al., 2008 and Maduekwe et al., 2015

claim: The expression of the SARS-COV2 receptor, ACE2 in club cells, and AT2 cells is increased in adult mice exposed to hyperoxia as neonates.
source: Furthermore, this effect seems independent of the pathogen, since Yee et al. have recently demonstrated that the expression of the SARS-COV2 receptor, ACE2 in club cells, and AT2 cells is increased in adult mice exposed to hyperoxia as neonates (Yee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yee et al., 2020

claim: Circadian rhythms offer protection against IAV, wherein mortality is threefold lower if animals are infected in the morning than in the evening.
source: We have previously demonstrated that circadian rhythms offer a protection against IAV, wherein mortality is threefold lower if the animals are infected in the morning than in the evening (Sengupta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sengupta et al., 2019

claim: Time of day-specific protection from IAV is lost upon global deletion of core clock gene, Bmal1, which exacerbates immunopathology independent of viral replication.
source: This time of day-specific protection is lost upon genetic disruption of the clock via global deletion of core clock gene, Bmal1, which exacerbates immunopathology independent of viral replication.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sengupta et al., 2019 in the previous sentence

claim: Changes in oxygen tension are known to affect the circadian clock.
source: Changes in oxygen tension are known to affect the clock (Walton et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walton et al., 2018 and Wu et al., 2017

claim: Low oxygen levels or hypoxia stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF).
source: Low oxygen levels or hypoxia stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hypoxia and HIF

claim: There exists a reciprocal relationship between the circadian clock and Hif1a mediated at the genomic level.
source: There exists a reciprocal relationship between the circadian clock and Hif1a mediated at the genomic level (Peek et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peek et al., 2017 and Wu et al., 2017

claim: A short burst of hypoxia was shown to desynchronize the relationship between the SCN and peripheral clocks.
source: More recently, even a short burst of hypoxia was shown to desynchronize the relationship between the SCN and peripheral clocks (Manella et al., 2020), which would confer further risk under conditions of stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to Manella et al., 2020

claim: The early neonatal period represents a critical window for the development and consolidation of circadian rhythms.
source: The early neonatal period represents a critical window for the development and consolidation of many important pathways, including circadian rhythms (Bartman et al., 2020; Rivkees, 2007; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartman et al., 2020, Rivkees, 2007, and Yang et al., 2014

claim: Early-life exposure to light, inflammation, or alcohol has disruptive effects on circadian rhythms in adulthood.
source: Early-life exposure to light (Coleman and Canal, 2017; Smarr et al., 2017), inflammation (Adler et al., 2014), or alcohol has disruptive effects on circadian rhythms in adulthood (Allen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coleman and Canal, 2017, Smarr et al., 2017, Adler et al., 2014, and Allen et al., 2005

claim: Mice infected at ZT11 (dusk) had threefold higher mortality than mice infected at ZT23 (dawn).
source: We previously showed that mice infected at ZT11 (ZT11 refers to 'Zeitgeber Time' 11 or dusk which marks the beginning of the active phase in mice since they are nocturnal) had threefold higher mortality than mice infected at ZT23 (dawn or at the beginning of their rest phase) (Sengupta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sengupta et al., 2019

claim: Room air control mice maintained the time of day difference in mortality, with the group infected at ZT11 having mortality 2.6 times higher than mice infected at ZT23 (survival 72% in ZT23 vs. 33% in ZT11, p<0.01).
source: The room air controls maintained the time of day difference in mortality; the group infected at ZT11 had a mortality 2.6 times higher than the mice infected at ZT23 (survival 72% in ZT23 vs. 33% in ZT11, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mice exposed to hyperoxia as neonates lost the time of day difference in mortality from IAV infection (survival in hyperoxia groups: ZT23 at 37% and ZT11 at 25%).
source: By contrast, the mice that had been exposed to hyperoxia as neonates lost this time of day difference: both groups had mortality comparable to the ZT11 (in RA) group (survival in hyperoxia groups: ZT23 at 37% and ZT11 at 25%; Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in text and Figure 1b and c

claim: Adult mice exposed to hyperoxia maintained the same difference in outcomes as seen in room air controls when infected with IAV at either ZT23 or ZT11.
source: However, when adult mice exposed to hyperoxia were infected with IAV at either ZT23 or ZT11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), they maintained the same difference in outcomes as seen in room air controls in Figure 2b and c.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in text and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Exposure to hyperoxia as adults did not appear to impair the circadian control over mortality and morbidity from IAV seen with exposure to neonatal hyperoxia.
source: Thus, exposure to hyperoxia as adults did not appear to impair the circadian control over mortality and morbidity from IAV seen with exposure to neonatal hyperoxia.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data comparing adult vs. neonatal hyperoxia exposure

claim: Early life (p0–p5) accords a unique window of influencing circadian regulation, and exposure to hyperoxia during this period disrupts circadian regulation of the lung injury response to IAV infection.
source: Considered together, this suggests that early life (p0–p5) accords a unique window of influencing circadian regulation and as such exposure to hyperoxia during this period disrupts circadian regulation of the lung injury response to IAV infection.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of neonatal vs. adult hyperoxia exposure effects

claim: Mice are born at the saccular stage of lung development that corresponds to 24–28 weeks gestation for humans.
source: Mice are born at the saccular stage of lung development that corresponds to 24–28 weeks gestation for humans (Warburton et al., 2010) and thus neonatal hyperoxia provides an excellent model to study BPD (Hilgendorff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Warburton et al., 2010 and Hilgendorff et al., 2014

claim: Neonatal hyperoxia provides an excellent model to study BPD.
source: Mice are born at the saccular stage of lung development that corresponds to 24–28 weeks gestation for humans (Warburton et al., 2010) and thus neonatal hyperoxia provides an excellent model to study BPD (Hilgendorff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hilgendorff et al., 2014

claim: Pups exposed to hyperoxia weigh less immediately after exposure but are indistinguishable from room air controls in weight or overall activity by 8–12 weeks of age.
source: Immediately after exposure, the pups exposed to hyperoxia weigh less (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). However, these pups are indistinguishable from the room air controls in weight or overall activity by 8–12 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The hyperoxia group displayed significantly more variation in their period lengths compared to room air controls.
source: Interestingly, while phase, period length, amplitude, and total activity patterns were comparable between the two groups, the hyperoxia group displayed significantly more variation in their period lengths (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2a

claim: Infection with IAV disrupts circadian locomotor rhythms in a mouse model of COPD.
source: Infection with IAV disrupts circadian locomotor rhythms under in a mouse model of COPD (Sundar et al., 2015), raising the possibility that further stress may unmask a central phenotype.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sundar et al., 2015

claim: Normoxia and hyperoxia groups did not entrain differently to changes in lighting schedule.
source: Normoxia and hyperoxia groups did not entrain differently to this small change (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2b and c

claim: The effects of neonatal hyperoxia on IAV infection are not mediated via lasting changes in the central clock.
source: Thus, considered together, these data are consistent with the hypothesis that effects of neonatal hyperoxia on IAV infection are not mediated via lasting changes in the central clock.
evidence: Inferred from the locomotor activity and entrainment data

claim: The total CD45+ population did not differ at ZT23 and ZT11 time points in the normoxia group.
source: While the total CD45+ population did not differ at these time points in the normoxia group, mice at ZT23 had higher numbers of CD45+ cells than at ZT11 in the hyperoxia group (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3a

claim: Mice at ZT23 had higher numbers of CD45+ cells than at ZT11 in the hyperoxia group.
source: While the total CD45+ population did not differ at these time points in the normoxia group, mice at ZT23 had higher numbers of CD45+ cells than at ZT11 in the hyperoxia group (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3a

claim: The percentage of natural killer (NK) cells was significantly lower in the hyperoxia-exposed mice at both time points.
source: The percentage of natural killer (NK) was significantly lower in the hyperoxia-exposed mice at both time points.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry

claim: The phase of the monocytes seems to reverse upon exposure to hyperoxia.
source: And the phase of the monocytes seems to reverse upon exposure to hyperoxia.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry

claim: More NK cells and lesser inflammatory monocytes were present in the group infected at ZT23 relative to the ZT11 group and thus associated with better outcomes.
source: Interestingly, in our previous work, more NK cells and lesser inflammatory monocytes were present in the group infected at ZT23 relative to the ZT11 group and thus associated with better outcomes (Sengupta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sengupta et al., 2019

claim: The viral burden was comparable between the groups infected at ZT11 or ZT23 in both neonatal hyperoxia- and room-air-exposed groups.
source: Consistent with our previous work, we found that the viral burden was comparable between the groups infected at ZT11 or ZT23; this held true in both neonatal hyperoxia- and room-air-exposed groups (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Animals infected in the hyperoxia group scored worse for lung injury and the time of day difference in severity was absent.
source: On histological analyses, animals infected in the hyperoxia group scored worse for lung injury and the time of day difference in severity was absent (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3c

claim: Among control animals exposed to room air as neonates, the room air group showed a higher total BAL count at ZT11 than at ZT23 by day 5 p.i.
source: Concordant with our previous work, among control animals exposed to room air as neonates, the room air group showed a higher total BAL count at ZT11 than at ZT23 by day 5 p.i. (Figure 3d) among control animals exposed to room air as neonates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3d

claim: Among the hyperoxia-exposed pups, the total BAL count was higher in the ZT11 than in the ZT23 group.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, this was not influenced by neonatal exposure to hyperoxia, since even among the hyperoxia-exposed pups, the total BAL count was higher in the ZT11 than in the ZT23 group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from BAL analysis

claim: Impaired circadian regulation of the response to IAV does not appear to arise directly from deficits in the circadian regulation of innate immunity.
source: Thus, impaired circadian regulation of the response to IAV does not appear to arise directly from deficits in the circadian regulation of innate immunity.
evidence: Inferred from the BAL count data showing maintained time-of-day differences

claim: Subtle differences in the phase of the oscillation of core clock genes Bmal1, Per2, and Nr1d2 were noted as a consequence of neonatal hyperoxia, but none of these changes were statistically significant.
source: On visual inspection, subtle differences in the phase of the oscillation of core clock genes Bmal1, Per2, and Nr1d2 were noted as a consequence of neonatal hyperoxia, but none of these changes were statistically significant (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4a

claim: The hyperoxia-exposed animals showed rhythmic expression of the Period2 gene with comparable periodicity and phase to the animals exposed to room air.
source: The hyperoxia-exposed animals showed rhythmic expression of the Period2 gene with comparable periodicity and phase to the animals exposed to room air.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Per2luc mice bioluminescence recordings

claim: The amplitude of Period2 oscillations was significantly dampened in the hyperoxia group.
source: However, the amplitude of these oscillations was significantly dampened in the hyperoxia group (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4b

claim: The perturbation induced by IAV infection unmasks a dysregulation of circadian function intrinsic to the lung in animals exposed to neonatal hyperoxia.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that the perturbation induced by IAV infection unmasks a dysregulation of circadian function intrinsic to the lung in animals exposed to neonatal hyperoxia.
evidence: Inferred from the dampened amplitude of Period2 oscillations in hyperoxia-exposed animals

claim: Neonatal hyperoxia disrupts the development of the respiratory epithelium, at least in part due to the depletion of AT2 cells after recovery.
source: Neonatal hyperoxia disrupts the development of the respiratory epithelium, at least in part due to the depletion of AT2 cells after recovery (Yee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yee et al., 2014

claim: During hyperoxia, the AT2 cell number expands as a source of AT1 cells; upon return to room air for recovery, there is a progressive depletion of AT2 cells, with approximately 70% surviving at 8 weeks of age.
source: During hyperoxia, the AT2 cell number expands as a source of AT1 cells; upon return to room air for recovery, there is a progressive depletion of AT2 cells, with approximately 70% surviving at 8 weeks of age (Yee et al., 2014; Yee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yee et al., 2014 and Yee et al., 2016

claim: In tamoxifen-treated SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl mice, Bmal1 expression was selectively absent in AT2 cells but not elsewhere such as the airway epithelium.
source: In the tamoxifen-treated SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl mice, Bmal1 expression was selectively absent in AT2 cells but not elsewhere such as the airway epithelium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Cre− mice infected in the morning had better survival than cre− mice infected in the evening (72% survival in CT23 group versus 20% survival in CT11 group; p<0.01).
source: While the cre− mice infected in the morning had better survival than cre− mice infected in the evening (Figure 5a; 72% survival in CT23 group versus 20% survival is CT11 group; p<0.01 by Mental–Cox test), this time of day difference was lost in mice lacking Bmal1 in their AT2 cells (Figure 5a; 25% survival in CT23 group versus 38% in the CT11 group of SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5a

claim: The time of day difference in survival was lost in mice lacking Bmal1 in their AT2 cells (25% survival in CT23 group versus 38% in the CT11 group of SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl).
source: While the cre− mice infected in the morning had better survival than cre− mice infected in the evening (Figure 5a; 72% survival in CT23 group versus 20% survival is CT11 group; p<0.01 by Mental–Cox test), this time of day difference was lost in mice lacking Bmal1 in their AT2 cells (Figure 5a; 25% survival in CT23 group versus 38% in the CT11 group of SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5a

claim: Post-natal deletion of Bmal1 specifically in AT2 epithelial cells recapitulated the impact of neonatal hyperoxia on IAV-induced mortality and morbidity.
source: Thus, post-natal deletion of Bmal1 specifically in AT2 epithelial cells thus recapitulated the impact of neonatal hyperoxia on IAV-induced mortality and morbidity.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl mice and neonatal hyperoxia-exposed mice

claim: The viral loads at days 1, 5, and 8 were comparable across genotypes in animals infected at CT11 or CT23.
source: We found that the viral loads at days 1 and 5 and day 8 were comparable across genotypes in animals infected at CT11 or CT23, both via hemagglutination inhibition assay (Figure 5c) and viral nucleic acid expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The lung pathology was worse in cre− group infected at CT11 than at CT23, but this time of day protection was lost in the cre+ animals, where the histology was worse at both CT11 and CT23.
source: While the lung pathology was worse in cre− group infected at CT11 than at CT23, this time of day protection was lost in the cre+ animals, where the histology was worse at both CT11 and CT23 (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5d

claim: Many of the gene expression signatures were comparable between the hyperoxia-treated animals and those with Bmal1 deleted in AT2 cells, including a reduction in Il1b and Il10 in both groups.
source: Furthermore, we found that many of the gene expression signatures were comparable between the hyperoxia-treated animals and those with Bmal1 deleted in AT2 cells. This included a reduction in Il1b and Il10 in both hyperoxia-exposed animals and cre+ mice, while the pattern of change was comparable for ccl2 (all on day 5 p.i. in Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6a

claim: Even with the loss of Bmal1 in AT2 cells (SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl), the BAL cell count varied by time of day, being higher in CT11 than at CT23 in both cre+ and cre− animals on day 5 p.i.
source: Finally, even with the loss of Bmal1 in AT2 cells (SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl), the BAL cell count varied by time of day (Figure 6b), being higher in CT11 than at CT23 in both cre+ and cre− animals on day 5 p.i. – again similar to the BAL count patterns seen in adults exposed to hyperoxia.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6b

claim: Early-life hyperoxia disrupts the circadian rhythm-mediated protection in IAV-induced lung injury through AT2-clock-mediated effects.
source: Considered together, these results support the possibility that early-life hyperoxia disrupts the circadian rhythm-mediated protection in IAV-induced lung injury through AT2-clock-mediated effects.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of hyperoxia-exposed animals and AT2-specific Bmal1 deletion

claim: Neonatal hyperoxia abolishes the clock-mediated time of day protection from IAV in mice, independent of viral burden through host tolerance pathways.
source: Here, we show that neonatal hyperoxia abolishes the clock-mediated time of day protection from IAV in mice, independent of viral burden through host tolerance pathways.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing comparable viral loads but different outcomes

claim: The lung intrinsic clock (and not the central or immune clocks) mediated the dysregulation caused by neonatal hyperoxia.
source: We discovered that the lung intrinsic clock (and not the central or immune clocks) mediated this dysregulation.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing intact central clock and immune responses but disrupted lung-specific effects

claim: Loss of circadian protein, Bmal1, in alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells recapitulates the increased mortality, loss of temporal gating, and other key features of hyperoxia-exposed animals.
source: Loss of circadian protein, Bmal1, in alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells recapitulates the increased mortality, loss of temporal gating, and other key features of hyperoxia-exposed animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from SftpcCreERt2/+::Bmal1fl/fl mice

claim: The circadian clock in AT2 cells mediates long-term effects of early-life exposures to the lungs.
source: Our data suggest a novel role for the circadian clock in AT2 cells in mediating long-term effects of early-life exposures to the lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing AT2-specific Bmal1 deletion recapitulates neonatal hyperoxia effects

claim: The SCN clock is well known to be resistant to non-photic stimuli.
source: This is not surprising – while other adverse effects early in life are known to disrupt local or central circadian rhythmicity (Coleman and Canal, 2017; Smarr et al., 2017), the SCN clock is well known to be resistant to non-photic stimuli (Damiola et al., 2000; Stokkan et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Damiola et al., 2000 and Stokkan et al., 2001

claim: Adults exposed to hyperoxia as neonates had a hyper-inflammatory response, with higher BAL counts in comparison to the room air controls according to O'Reilly et al.
source: This is in contrast with the work of O'Reilly et al. who have shown that adults exposed to hyperoxia as neonates had a hyper-inflammatory response, with higher BAL counts in comparison to the room air controls.
evidence: Supported by reference to O'Reilly et al.'s work

claim: Both clock and HIF belong to the same basic helix-loop-helix PER-ARNT-SIM (bHLH-PAS) transcription factor super family.
source: Interestingly, both clock and HIF belong to the same basic helix-loop-helix PER-ARNT-SIM (bHLH-PAS) transcription factor super family.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about transcription factor families

claim: In the skeletal muscle, a reciprocal relationship was noted between the hypoxia-sensing HIF1 pathways and the circadian clock – the response to hypoxia is gated by the circadian clock and HIF1α binds to clock targets to modulate the clock output under hypoxic conditions.
source: In the skeletal muscle, a reciprocal relationship was noted between the hypoxia-sensing HIF1 pathways and the circadian clock – the response to hypoxia is gated by the circadian clock and HIF1α binds to clock targets to modulate the clock output under hypoxic conditions (Peek et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peek et al., 2017

claim: HIF1α is shown to accelerate adaptation to jetlag, suggesting an interaction between HIF1α and the circadian clock at a central level.
source: Furthermore, HIF1α is shown to accelerate adaptation to jetlag, suggesting an interaction between the two at a central level (Adamovich et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adamovich et al., 2017

claim: Hypoxia was shown to desynchronize the relationship between peripheral tissue clocks.
source: More recently, hypoxia was shown to desynchronize the relationship between peripheral tissue clocks (Manella et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manella et al., 2020

claim: A unique window exists in the lung in the early neonatal period that might affect circadian regulation throughout later life.
source: Our work here suggests that a unique window exists in the lung in the early neonatal period that might affect circadian regulation throughout later life.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing stage-specific effects of hyperoxia

claim: Many developmental pathways such as the Wnt-βcatenin pathways have recently been demonstrated to be central to the pathogenesis of BPD following neonatal hyperoxia.
source: Many developmental pathways such as the Wnt-βcatenin pathways have recently been demonstrated to be central to the pathogenesis of BPD following neonatal hyperoxia (Sucre et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sucre et al., 2020

claim: Neonatal hyperoxia affects multiple transcription factors such as Nfe212, Cdnk1a, Fos, Trp53, Rela, Stat3, and Cebpa.
source: Neonatal hyperoxia affects multiple transcription factors such as Nfe212, Cdnk1a, Fos, Trp53, Rela, Stat3, and Cebpa (Wright and Dennery, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright and Dennery, 2009

claim: Many transcription factors affected by neonatal hyperoxia are known to be under circadian control.
source: Many of these transcription factors and pathways are known to be under circadian control.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about circadian regulation of transcription factors

claim: Children born prematurely and suffering from even mild BPD have persistent adverse effects on their lung function into adulthood.
source: In conclusion, children born prematurely and suffering from even mild BPD have persistent adverse effects on their lung function into adulthood.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge about BPD outcomes

claim: Long-lasting damage to circadian mechanisms residing in AT2 cells may result in part from persistent adverse effects on lung function in children with BPD.
source: This may result in part from long-lasting damage to circadian mechanisms residing in AT2 cells that influence the response to injury after viral infection.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the experimental findings

claim: Bmal1 is the only circadian gene whose sole deletion is sufficient to cause arrhythmicity of locomotor activity.
source: Although many clock genes participate in the generation and maintenance of circadian rhythms, Bmal1 is the only circadian gene whose sole deletion is sufficient to cause arrhythmicity of locomotor activity – the hallmark of circadian disruption.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Bmal1 function

claim: Embryonic deletion of Bmal1 results in a severe accelerated aging phenotype, in which the circadian phenotype is confounded by potentially off target developmental effects of Bmal1 deletion.
source: Embryonic deletion of Bmal1 results in a severe accelerated aging phenotype, in which the circadian phenotype is confounded by potentially off target developmental effects of Bmal1 deletion (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016

claim: This is the first report of a cell intrinsic clock in AT2 cells.
source: We and others (Gibbs et al., 2014; Sengupta et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019) have demonstrated a role for the Scgb1a1 (or CCSP) clock in mediating lung injury, however, this is the first report of a cell intrinsic clock in AT2 cells.
evidence: Claimed as a novel finding by the authors

claim: The Scgb1a1-cre models affect AT2 cells as well.
source: Since many of the Scgb1a1-cre models affect AT2 cells as well (Rawlins et al., 2009), it is possible that the Scgb1a1-cre described previously overestimates the effect of Bmal1 deletion.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rawlins et al., 2009 and inference from current findings

claim: Hyperoxia exposure in adult mice changes the circadian gene expression.
source: While we focused on long-term effects of neonatal hyperoxia on circadian networks, Lagishetty et al. has suggested that hyperoxia exposure in adult mice changes the circadian gene expression, although only a single time point was assessed (Lagishetty et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lagishetty et al., 2014
